bib.title: Building knowledge graphs with large language models (Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action, ch. 6)

question: How do you turn LLM-extracted entities and relations from a historical archive into a normalized, entity-resolved knowledge graph and analyse it?
contributions: Normalization and graph-based entity resolution baseline
Influence-network analysis with PageRank, betweenness, few-hop queries

results.claim: The book's RAC project had more than 10,000 pages; the chapter's example uses 150 pages of Warren Weaver's 1939 diary.
results.quote: We had more than 10,000 pages for this project, but for this example, we selected a subset of 150 pages of Warren Weaver's diary.

results.claim: Off-the-shelf coreference models could not resolve the program officers' shortened names, while GPT did the NER, entity resolution and RE implicitly.
results.setup: RAC diaries with abbreviations such as 'S.' and 'U.Cal.'; models tested not named, no scores
results.quote: None of the off-the-shelf coreference models we tested could resolve these shortened names into canonical forms.

results.claim: Graph is built in three layers (document, metagraph, KG) so normalization and entity resolution happen before the final KG; the KG can be rebuilt from the metagraph.
results.quote: Unmerged GPT entities ( Entity nodes) and relations among them, as well as their linkage to the original page from

results.claim: Baseline person resolution: link mentions with META_PERSONS_SIMILAR by string similarity plus relatedness, run weakly connected components, name each group by its longest member.
results.quote: For each WCC group, select a common name to represent it: we choose the longest one

results.claim: Occupations were clustered via GPT or SentenceBERT embeddings with agglomerative clustering, reported as giving very good or best results, without numbers.
results.quote: We’ve gotten the best results by creating embeddings of Occupations

results.claim: The cyclotron influence query surfaced Laurence Irving through an RE failure (name misspelled as Lawrence), so a validation feedback loop is needed.
results.quote: This is an important re‐ minder that LLMs are not magic; they do make mistakes, and sometimes silly ones.

results.claim: ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo was used to find diary entry boundaries (typically under three pages) for multipage processing.
results.quote: we used ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo to iden‐ tify the boundaries of individual diary entries, which typically contain fewer than three pages

limits: Illustrated on 150 pages of one diary; no accuracy, precision or recall numbers anywhere.
Entity resolution is a baseline; full discussion declared out of scope; grants linking and Conversation nodes are future work.
Models, prompts and thresholds are not given; code is in the book's repository, not the chapter.
Chapter admits GPT RE errors (Irving/Lawrence) and a Langmuir duplicate node left unresolved.
practices: Create (not merge) entity mentions per page in a metagraph so the KG can be rebuilt and every fact traced to source text (6.1.2).
Normalize before resolving: strip titles from Person names, lowercase Occupation names into name_normalized (6.1.3, Listing 6.1).
Use a stopword list (e.g. Foundation) before creating similarity links (6.1.4 tip).
Combine string similarity with graph signals (shared employer, topic, Louvain community) for resolution (6.1.4).
Resolve connected mentions with weakly connected components and pick the longest name as canonical (6.1.4).
Cluster Occupation embeddings with agglomerative clustering for semantic similarity (6.1.4, 6.3).
Build an analyst feedback loop to validate or reject graph content (6.2).
Chunk by page for short corpora; detect entry boundaries for multipage documents (6.1.2, 6.3).
